versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 18 When Jared was 162 years old, he became the father of Enoch. 19 And after he had become the father of Enoch, Jared lived 800 years and had other sons and daughters. 20 So Jared lived a total of 962 years, and then he died.

21 When Enoch was 65 years old, he became the father of Methuselah. 22 And after he had become the father of Methuselah, Enoch walked with God 300 years and had other sons and daughters. 23 So Enoch lived a total of 365 years.
24 Enoch walked with God, and then he was no more, because God had taken him away.

context_lines: Jared's entry follows the familiar pattern: a son, more children, years of life, and death. Enoch's entry interrupts it. Genesis twice says he walked with God and closes by saying God took him. The expected notice of death is absent. That difference is the main reason this short entry stands out among the surrounding names.

Enoch has a family and walks with God over many years. The passage places that faithfulness within ordinary human life, not apart from it. It does not record the date of his conversion or explain all that happened when God took him. For the Christian explanation of that ending, Hebrews 11 supplies the clearest direct comment.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly read Enoch's walk as a life pleasing to God and his being taken as an exception to the deaths around him. [Hebrews 11:5–6](https://biblehub.com/bsb/hebrews/11.htm) states that he was taken without experiencing death and uses him to explain why faith is essential to pleasing God.
god_plan_lines: Enoch belongs in Hebrews' account of people who trusted God before receiving the full outcome of His promises. [Hebrews 11:5–6, 39–40](https://biblehub.com/bsb/hebrews/11.htm) connects his experience with that larger community of faith and with the better fulfillment God has prepared. Genesis's brief exception is not left as an unexplained curiosity.

There is also a helpful parallel with the promised transformation of believers who are alive when Christ comes. [1 Corinthians 15:51–54](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_corinthians/15.htm) says that not everyone will die, but all will be changed. Enoch's story shows God's power to take a person without death; Paul states the future promise. The comparison does not, by itself, set a timetable for the church's rescue or explain its relation to every future judgment.
current_position_lines: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.
